chapters.title: Commodity Markets in India — Structure and Players

lessons.title: Who Trades Commodities — Hedgers, Speculators, Arbitrageurs, and FPIs

markDefs.definition: The total number of outstanding futures or options contracts in a given commodity that have not yet been closed out, settled, or delivered. It measures how much money and risk is actively parked in a contract, distinct from trading volume.

children.text: figure for MCX Gold on any given day and you are looking at a number built by very different people with very different reasons for being there. A jewellery manufacturer in Rajkot has sold gold futures to lock in his input cost. A retail trader on Zerodha's Kite has gone long because he expects prices to rise before Diwali. A proprietary trading desk is running a spread between two contract months, indifferent to which way gold actually moves. And since 2022, there is a real chance a foreign portfolio investor is also sitting somewhere in that open interest figure, a category of participant that did not legally exist in Indian commodity derivatives a decade ago. This lesson is about all four.

body.text: A commodity futures market only functions because it mixes participants with opposite needs: some want to shed real price risk, some want to take it on for profit, some want to arbitrage inconsistencies away, and a growing group of institutional and foreign players now sit alongside all three. SEBI treats each group differently, mainly through how it sets position limits.

markDefs.definition: SEBI's formal category for hedgers: manufacturers, traders, farmers, farmer producer organisations (FPOs), processors and exporters who have genuine, demonstrable exposure to a commodity's price through their actual business, and who are therefore eligible for higher hedge position limits than a purely speculative client.

children.text: SEBI groups genuine hedgers under a specific label:

(VCPs). The idea is simple: if you can show you are actually exposed to a commodity's price through your business, you are allowed to hold a larger futures position than someone speculating with no such exposure, because your position is offsetting a real risk rather than creating a new one.

body.caption: Value Chain Participants: who they are and what they hedge

cells: Producers and farmers
A guar or mustard farmer, or a Farmer Producer Organisation (FPO) in Rajasthan or Madhya Pradesh
The risk of prices falling before or at harvest
Processors and manufacturers
An edible oil refiner, a jewellery manufacturer, a spinning mill buying raw cotton
The cost of raw material rising before it is processed and sold
Traders and stockists
A bullion dealer or an agri commodity trading house holding physical inventory
The value of inventory already held falling before it is sold
Exporters and importers
A textile exporter, a company importing crude or base metals
Currency-linked and global-price-linked cost or revenue swings on a confirmed order

body.text: Being a VCP is not automatic just because your business happens to use a commodity. You have to declare and demonstrate your underlying exposure to get the higher hedge limit. This documentation requirement is exactly what Chapter 3 walks through when it covers how a real hedge is actually set up.

children.text: Speculators and How Position Limits Actually Work

A speculator, from a retail trader with a ₹50,000 account to a large proprietary trading desk, has no such underlying exposure to point to, so they are held to standard client-level position limits. As of the framework SEBI put in force in September 2026, every commodity is classified by how liquid and deliverable it is, and the client-level position limit is set as a percentage of the market-wide open interest in that commodity:

body.caption: Client-level position limits by commodity classification (in force from September 2026)
headers: Why the limit is tighter or looser

cells: Broad
2% of market-wide open interest
Deep, liquid contracts where a single client's position is unlikely to move the market
Narrow
1% of market-wide open interest
Moderately liquid contracts, where concentration risk is a bigger concern
Sensitive
0.5% of market-wide open interest
Thin markets, often agricultural, where one large position could distort the price or squeeze other participants

body.title: Why classify commodities at all?
body.question: Why does SEBI give a 'Sensitive' commodity a tighter client-level position limit (0.5%) than a 'Broad' commodity (2%)?
options: Sensitive commodities are always more expensive per lot
Sensitive commodities tend to be thinly traded, so one large position can distort prices or squeeze the market, unlike a deep, liquid Broad commodity
It is a fixed rule with no relationship to liquidity
Broad commodities are riskier, so they need looser limits to allow hedging
body.explanation: The classification is about market depth and manipulation risk, not price or contract value. A thinly traded, Sensitive commodity is far easier for one large position to distort than a deep, liquid, Broad one, so the limit is set tighter to protect market integrity.

body.text: The same September 2026 reform also capped the monetary penalty for a position limit breach at ₹2 lakh for larger violations, instead of scaling it without limit. Regulators had heard that genuine hedgers were under-hedging or avoiding the market altogether for fear of an inadvertent, disproportionate penalty. Rules like this are a reminder that commodity market regulation keeps evolving; always check the latest exchange circular for the limit that actually applies to you.

children.text: Arbitrageurs are usually institutional or proprietary desks, because the profit on any single arbitrage trade is small and needs speed and scale to matter. Two forms show up constantly in Indian commodities. Inter-exchange arbitrage trades the same commodity across markets, for instance buying gold on MCX while selling an equivalent position abroad when the rupee-adjusted prices drift apart. Calendar spread arbitrage trades the price gap between two expiry months of the same contract on the same exchange, betting that an unusually wide or narrow gap will normalise. You will see calendar spreads properly in Chapter 4.
The Newest Entrants: Foreign Portfolio Investors
Foreign participation in Indian commodity derivatives arrived in two distinct steps, and a third is currently on the table.

body.title: Foreign access to Indian commodity derivatives

events.title: Eligible Foreign Entities can hedge
events.description: SEBI allows foreign entities with genuine economic exposure to Indian commodities, such as a foreign company that actually buys or sells that commodity, to hedge that exposure using Indian commodity derivatives. This is access for hedging only, not general trading.

events.title: FPIs allowed into cash-settled, non-agri contracts
events.description: SEBI permits registered Foreign Portfolio Investors to participate in exchange-traded commodity derivatives for the first time, limited to cash-settled, non-agricultural commodity derivatives and indices built on them. This opens the door to speculative and portfolio-style participation, not just hedging a known exposure.

events.title: A proposal to go further
events.description: SEBI issues a consultation paper proposing to let FPIs also trade physically-settled non-agri contracts (including crude oil, natural gas, gold, silver and base metals), with safeguards requiring them to square off or roll over positions before the delivery period begins, so they never end up holding physical delivery obligations.

body.text: The August 2026 proposal is a consultation paper, not a final rule, as of this writing. Regulatory access for FPIs in commodity derivatives has genuinely expanded twice already and may expand again, so verify the current circular on SEBI's or the exchange's website rather than assuming today's rules are permanent.

body.title: Four traders, one contract
body.scenario: On the same day, four positions are opened in MCX Crude Oil futures. A Gujarat-based petrochemical manufacturer buys futures to lock in the cost of crude-linked feedstock for a confirmed production run. A college graduate trading from his phone buys futures purely because he read that OPEC+ might cut supply. A trading firm buys MCX crude while selling an equivalent position on an overseas exchange, having spotted a rupee-adjusted pricing gap between the two. A registered Foreign Portfolio Investor, trading the cash-settled MCX crude oil index, takes a view on oil prices as part of a global multi-asset strategy.
body.prompt: Identify each participant's role (hedger, speculator, arbitrageur, or FPI participant) and explain how SEBI's position-limit treatment would likely differ between the manufacturer and the college graduate.
body.modelAnswer: The petrochemical manufacturer is a hedger, and if the underlying exposure is declared and verified, would qualify as a Value Chain Participant eligible for a higher hedge position limit than a standard client. The college graduate is a speculator with no underlying exposure, subject to the standard client-level limit (Broad, Narrow or Sensitive, depending on how crude oil is classified) with no special allowance. The trading firm is an arbitrageur, profiting from the price gap rather than betting on crude's direction. The FPI is participating as an institutional investor under the cash-settled, non-agri access route opened in September 2022, most likely for portfolio or speculative purposes rather than hedging a specific physical exposure.

cards.definition: The total number of outstanding futures or options contracts in a commodity that have not been closed out, settled, or delivered.
SEBI's classification for hedgers with genuine, declared exposure to a commodity through their business, eligible for higher hedge position limits.
The maximum position a client can hold in a contract, set as a percentage of market-wide open interest, tighter for thinner (Sensitive) commodities and looser for deep (Broad) ones.
A foreign entity with genuine economic exposure to an Indian commodity, permitted since 2018 to hedge that specific exposure using Indian commodity derivatives.
A registered FPI permitted, since September 2022, to trade cash-settled non-agricultural Indian commodity derivatives, without needing to prove hedging exposure.

points: Every commodity futures contract's open interest is a mix of hedgers, speculators, arbitrageurs and, increasingly, foreign institutional participants.
Genuine hedgers who declare real underlying exposure are classified as Value Chain Participants and get higher position limits than speculative clients.
Speculators face standard client-level position limits, set as a percentage of market-wide open interest that is tighter for thinly traded, Sensitive commodities and looser for deep, Broad ones.
Arbitrageurs, usually institutional, trade price gaps across exchanges or across contract months rather than betting on direction.

Foreign participation has expanded in stages: hedging-only access for Eligible Foreign Entities from 2018, cash-settled non-agri access for registered FPIs from September 2022, and a 2026 proposal (not yet final) to extend FPIs into physically-settled non-agri contracts.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Position limits, hedge classifications and eligibility rules for different participant categories change through SEBI and exchange circulars; always confirm the current rules before trading or attempting to claim hedger status.
